title: Hope as a Skill
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A doctor imprisoned in a camp noticed that between Christmas 1944 and New Year’s more prisoners died than ever before, even though the hunger and the labor hadn’t changed. Something else had: many had lived with a quiet belief that they would be home for Christmas. When Christmas passed, they lay down and faded. The camp doctor recorded that it wasn’t typhus that killed them, but the loss of hope, which stripped their bodies of resistance. Hope isn’t a decoration on life. It is its load-bearing structure.

Psychology has also discovered the other half of this truth: helplessness can be learned, because anyone who has repeatedly experienced that their effort changes nothing stops trying, even when the way out stands wide open. But if helplessness can be learned, so can hope. The difference lies not in the facts but in how we explain them: after a failure, the pessimist says “always, everything, me,” while the optimist says “temporary, this one thing, many causes.” So cross-examine a dark thought like a prosecutor: What’s the evidence? Is it really “never”? What does this actually mean for tomorrow? Researchers break hope down into three parts: a goal, a path, and agency. Cut the goal into steps so small it’s almost embarrassing, because every step you complete is proof that control exists. When a path collapses, sketch backup routes. Practice agency on things that are sure to succeed. And in the evening, write down three good things from the day, because good things are like feathers: light and easy to miss. Watch your information diet too, because scrolling through nothing but alarms is training in helplessness, and hope, like any mood, is contagious: one person saying “let’s try it this way” changes the temperature of a whole household.

Biblical hope differs from optimism in one thing: it isn’t a weather forecast but trust in a Person. The author of Lamentations looked at the ruins of Jerusalem, and it was right there that he wrote that he calls one thing to mind and therefore has hope: the mercies of the LORD never fail; they are new every morning. Hope, like an anchor, holds not because the sea is calm, but because it reaches a seabed the storm can’t touch. Hope can be learned. But first, it can be received.

quote.text: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace as you believe in Him, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

questions: How do you explain your failures to yourself: “always, everything, me,” or “temporary, this one thing, many causes”?
What is your hope standing on, and would it survive a night when everything else fails?

paragraphs: A doctor imprisoned in a concentration camp noticed a phenomenon that medicine couldn’t explain. Between Christmas 1944 and New Year’s, more prisoners died than ever before, even though neither the starvation rations, nor the weather, nor the labor had changed. Something else had: many prisoners had lived with a quiet belief that they would be home for Christmas. When Christmas came and went and no liberation came, people lay down on their bunks and faded. It wasn’t typhus or hunger that killed them, the doctor wrote, but the loss of hope, which stripped their bodies of resistance. This observation, recorded in one of the most important books of the twentieth century, says something that laboratories confirm today: hope isn’t a decoration on life. It is its load-bearing structure.

The other half of this truth was discovered in the 1960s, unfortunately first in animals. Dogs that had repeatedly been subjected to unpleasant stimuli with no way to escape stopped trying to escape even when the way out stood wide open: they lay there and endured it, even though all they had to do was jump over a low barrier. Researchers called this learned helplessness and soon recognized the same mechanism in people: anyone who has repeatedly experienced that their effort changes nothing eventually stops trying, even when circumstances have long since changed. Helplessness turned out to be learnable. But within this grim discovery lay a spark: if helplessness can be learned, then so can hope. And this may be the most important news in modern psychology: hope isn’t a character trait that some are born with and others aren’t. It is a skill. And skills can be practiced.

It’s worth noticing, too, that today you can learn helplessness without living through any disaster yourself. An information diet made up of nothing but alarms is enough. News outlets and media live off our attention, and nothing grabs attention more reliably than a threat, so they feed us a world in which everything is falling apart and we have no influence over anything, because no one sends breaking-news alerts about things that got fixed, built, or went well. A person who scrolls through such news for hours is training exactly the same reflex as the dog behind the barrier: why bother trying? That’s why the hygiene of hope starts with something mundane, with your diet: less scrolling through alarms, more news on a human scale that you can influence, meaning your own street, your community, and your family.

Where exactly does the difference lie between a person of hope and a person of resignation? Not in the facts, but in the way they explain them. After a failure, the pessimist says three things: it’s permanent, as in “it will always be like this”; it’s pervasive, as in “everything is falling apart for me”; and it’s me, as in “because I’m hopeless.” The optimist says of the very same failure: it’s temporary, it concerns this one thing, and it had many causes, of which my part is only one. Notice: none of these statements changes the facts. What they change is the verdict, and the verdict decides whether a person will try again tomorrow. The good news is that you can catch your own explanatory style and translate it into a fairer one. The method is simple and resembles a courtroom trial. When a dark thought speaks up in your head, something like “I’ll never recover from this,” treat it not as the truth but as a prosecutor, and begin the cross-examination: What’s the evidence? Is it really “never,” when I’ve picked myself up before? What other explanations are there? What does this actually mean for tomorrow? This isn’t wishful thinking or pasting on a smile. It’s a fairer weighing of the evidence, because dark thoughts almost always convict without evidence.

Modern researchers break hope down into three parts, and this anatomy is very practical. Hope is a goal I can see, a path to it I can make out, and agency, meaning the belief that I can take the next step. When hope collapses, it’s usually a failure of one of these three parts, not all of them at once. Sometimes the goal is too big and needs to be cut into steps so small it’s almost embarrassing, because every step you complete is proof that control exists, and proof heals helplessness more effectively than encouragement. Sometimes the path has caved in, and you need to sit down with a sheet of paper and ask: which other way? People of hope don’t have better weather; they have more backup routes sketched out. And sometimes agency is lacking, and then it’s best to start with something tiny that is sure to succeed, because hope, like a muscle, grows through successful repetitions. A powerful yet underrated resource here is your own past: keep a journal of the storms you’ve weathered. Most of us have already been through things that at the time looked like the end of the world, only we don’t remember them, because crises we got through safely don’t hurt and don’t remind us of themselves. A written list of “what hasn’t killed me yet and what helped back then” is, in your darkest hour, hard evidence against the prosecutor who says, “You’ll never make it.” Add to this two power sources. Gratitude: good things are like feathers, light and easy to miss, so you have to collect them deliberately, for instance by writing down in the evening three things that went well that day, and why. And people: when your own faith is flickering out, someone else’s can be the spark, which is why hope is built around tables where someone believes in you. Remember the research on three links, which found that moods spread through human networks like waves? There’s much to suggest that hope travels the same way. One person on a team, in a classroom, or in a family who says “let’s try it this way” changes the temperature of the whole room, and that is a role waiting to be taken up in every home: to be the one from whom others catch not panic but calm. It’s no accident that people with strong hope are healthier, less likely to fall into depression, and live longer: the body listens to what the mind says about the future.

We also need to be honest about the limits of these exercises. Explanatory style and goals cut into steps work as long as the storm is moderate. But there come nights in life when all three parts of hope go dark at once: a diagnosis, the death of a loved one, the ruin of everything you’ve built. Then the question is no longer “How should I think about failure?” but “What is my hope standing on at all?” Optimism built on the idea that things will work out somehow, because they usually have, is a house built on sand: it stands until a flood comes that was never in the statistics. People of faith go through the same floods as everyone else, but they have somewhere to set their feet when the floor of their own strength gives way. And here psychology honestly yields the floor to something older than itself.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Hope isn’t an inborn trait but a skill: helplessness can be learned, so hope can be too. The difference between hope and resignation lies not in the facts but in how we explain them: the pessimist says of a failure “always, everything, me,” the optimist “temporary, this one thing, many causes.” Cross-examine dark thoughts like a prosecutor with no evidence. Build hope itself out of three parts: a goal cut into small steps, backup routes sketched out when the first path collapses, and agency practiced on things that are sure to succeed. Fuel it with gratitude, by writing down three good things from the day each evening, and with people, because when your own faith is flickering out, someone else’s can be the spark, and hope spreads through homes and teams like any mood. Watch your information diet too, because scrolling through nothing but alarms is training in helplessness. The body listens to what the mind says about the future: people of hope are healthier and live longer.

sections.heading: Look Higher
paragraphs: Biblical hope differs from optimism in one fundamental way: it isn’t a weather forecast but trust in a Person. The author of Lamentations looked at Jerusalem in ashes, at the ruins of everything he loved, and it was right there that he wrote a sentence that may be the boldest act of hope in all of world literature: “Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” Notice the mechanics of this sentence: he doesn’t feel hope; he calls it to mind, by a deliberate choice to remember God’s faithfulness. The Letter to the Hebrews calls such hope an anchor for the soul: an anchor holds a ship not because the sea is calm, but because it is fastened to a seabed the storm can’t reach. For the exiles in Babylon, in turn, a word was waiting: I know the plans I have for you, plans to prosper you, to give you a future and a hope. And all of this rests on an event, not a mood: Christians speak of hope so calmly not because they have sunnier temperaments, but because in the history of the world there was one morning when a tomb turned out to be empty. If the greatest of all nights didn’t have the last word, no other night has it either. This whole series is called BeHopeful precisely because that is the Bible’s message from its first page to its last. Hope can be learned, but first, it can simply be received.

questions: How do you explain your failures to yourself: “always, everything, me,” or “temporary, this one thing, many causes”?
What is your hope standing on, and would it survive a night when everything else fails?
Who around you is most in need of hope today, and how could you lend them a little of yours?
